stem: Jasper is a 2-year-old boy with asthma who presents with a 1-week history of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms followed by increasing cough and wheeze over 2 days. He has fever (39°C), tachycardia, tachypnoea, room-air oxygen saturation of 90%, and focal right lower zone bronchial breath sounds, reduced air entry, crackles, and dullness to percussion. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The combination of fever, hypoxaemia, focal chest signs (bronchial breath sounds, crackles, dullness), and reduced air entry is most consistent with lobar pneumonia rather than asthma. Asthma usually causes diffuse wheeze without focal percussion dullness or bronchial breath sounds.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: Preserved existing options; only one option is clearly correct based on the focal infective chest signs.

optionExplanations.A: Asthma would typically cause diffuse wheeze and prolonged expiration, not focal dullness and bronchial breathing.
optionExplanations.B: Correct: focal signs plus fever and hypoxia strongly suggest pneumonia.
optionExplanations.C: Cardiac failure can cause respiratory distress, but focal right lower zone findings and fever are more in keeping with pneumonia.
optionExplanations.D: Bronchiolitis usually occurs in younger infants and causes widespread crackles/wheeze rather than focal lobar signs.
optionExplanations.E: A foreign body can cause unilateral signs, but fever and crackles/dullness after a URI are more suggestive of pneumonia.

Clinical scenario 4 - Jasper

Jasper, a two year old boy with asthma, presents to the emergency department with a one week history of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms, followed by increasing coughing and wheezing over the past two days. His mother has been giving him regular salbutamol.

His vital signs are: RR 40/min, HR 150/min, Temp 39ºC and SaO

2

90% in room air.

Bronchial breath sounds are present in the right lower zone, with reduced air entry and occasional crackles. There is mild dullness to percussion over the right lower zone.

The following five questions refer to Jasper's clinical scenario.
